I also need a basemap showing terrain and roads. How should I set up the data sources in MapLibre — do I need vector tiles, or can I use GeoJSON?

*Use a hosted vector-tile basemap for terrain + roads, and keep your 8 000 trail segments in a separate **GeoJSON source** – as long as the file stays under ~5 MB (or you can simplify it a bit). If the file grows larger or you notice a noticeable pause when the map first loads, switch the trails to a tiny vector-tile set generated with **tippecanoe** (or Planetiler).*
Below is a step-by-step rationale, the concrete source set-up you can copy into your style, and the “what-if-it-gets-bigger” fallback.
## 1️⃣ Why GeoJSON is OK for ~8 000 trail segments

column1: *Result*: The whole file is downloaded once, parsed in < 1 s on a typical desktop and < 2 s on most mobiles. The map stays responsive, and you get full access to each feature’s properties for pop-ups, filtering, or editing.

> **Rule of thumb from the skill** – GeoJSON is “sweet spot” for **< 2 MB / < 5 000 features** and still works comfortably up to **~5 MB / ~5 000–10 000 features**. Anything larger pushes you into the “Lag zone”. Your 8 000-segment dataset is right at the top of that zone, so it’s a good candidate for GeoJSON *if* you keep the file size modest.
### How to keep the file small
1. **Simplify geometry** – `mapshaper -simplify 10%` or similar. Trail lines don’t need sub-meter precision at typical web-map zoom levels.
2. **Drop unnecessary properties** – keep only `name`, `distance`, maybe `difficulty`. Anything else just adds bytes.
3. **Compress the file** – serve it gzipped (most CDNs/servers do this automatically). A 4 MB GeoJSON often becomes ~1 MB over the wire.
If after these steps the file is still > 5 MB or you notice a noticeable “pause” on load, move to vector tiles (see §2).
## 2️⃣ When you *should* switch to vector tiles

column3: Why vector tiles help
Only the tiles that intersect the viewport are fetched, so the initial download is tiny.

column2: **Future growth** (you expect > 10 000 trails or more attributes)
column3: Tile generation is a one-time cost; the client never sees the full dataset.

column2: **Zoom-dependent styling** (e.g., thicker lines at high zoom, different colors per difficulty)
column3: You can set different `minzoom`/`maxzoom` on the same source-layer without re-encoding separate files.
You can bundle a single PMTiles archive (≈ 10 – 30 MB) and serve it locally.

A 180 MB / ≈ 400 k-polygon GeoJSON is far beyond the practical limits of MapLibre’s **geojson** source. The browser has to download, parse, and keep the whole file in memory, which almost always ends in long stalls or crashes.
**Solution:** Convert the data to **vector tiles** (or, if you only need a static picture, to a raster/image source) and add that tile source to your style. The vector-tile workflow gives you:
* Only the features that intersect the current viewport are fetched.
* Orders-of-magnitude smaller payloads (often < 1 KB per tile).
Below is a step-by-step checklist that tells you exactly what to do, which tools to use, and where to read the details. No full build script is provided – just the “what” and “where”.
## 1. Why GeoJSON Won’t Work for 180 MB / 400 k polygons

column1: anti-pattern — merging basemap and application data into one tileset,skills/maplibre-tile-sources/SKILL.md,"I want my roads, water, labels, and my own delivery-zone polygons all in a single vector tileset so the map only hits one source. What's the best pipeline to merge OpenStreetMap data with my polygons and build that combined tileset?
,**Short answer – you don’t need a “single-source” tileset for a normal web app.**
The usual, most maintainable pattern is:
1. **Use a hosted (or self-hosted) vector-tile basemap** that already contains roads, water, land-use, place-names, etc.
2. **Add your delivery-zone polygons as a second source** – either a `geojson` source (if the dataset is small) or a tiny vector-tile source that you generate yourself.

MapLibre will request both sources in parallel, composite the layers in the order you specify, and there is **no per-source rendering penalty**.  This keeps the basemap up-to-date, respects OSM licensing, and avoids having to rebuild the whole world every time a delivery zone changes.
## When a single combined tileset *is* justified
Only a few edge cases truly need “one source”:

column3: Why a single tileset might make sense

column2: **Offline / air-gapped kiosk** – no network at all.
column3: You must ship everything in one archive.

column2: **Demo / proof-of-concept** that must run from a single file.
column3: Simplicity for a short-lived demo.

column2: **Very small, static area** (e.g., a single city) where you control both the basemap and the overlay and you never need to update either.
column3: Building a tiny combined tileset is cheap.

column1: If you are in one of those scenarios, the pipeline below shows the *high-level* steps and the tools you would use.  **Do not copy-paste a full script – just follow the flow and read the linked docs for each tool.**

column3: Why it’s useful for this job
Reads OSM PBF directly, lets you add arbitrary GeoJSON layers, and writes a single PMTiles archive. Handles per-zoom simplification automatically.
Very fast for pure GeoJSON → vector tiles. If you first export OSM to GeoJSON (via `osmium export` or `osm2geojson`), you can concatenate your zones and tippecanoe everything in one command.
Packs the whole tileset into a single file that can be served via HTTP range requests – perfect for offline or “single-file” deployments.

column1: 1. **Licensing & attribution** – OSM data is **ODbL**. When you redistribute a combined tileset you must:
* Include the OSM attribution in your map UI.
* Provide a way for users to access the original OSM data (e.g., a link to the extract you used).
* Keep the attribution visible even if you “bake” the data into a single tileset.

2. **Update frequency** – Every time a delivery-zone polygon changes you would have to **re-run the whole build** (OSM + your data) and redeploy the tiles. With a two-source pattern you only need to replace the small `zones` source.

3. **Tile size & zoom levels** – Adding your polygons to a global OSM tileset can bloat the tiles at high zooms. Use tippecanoe/Planetiler options like `--drop-densest-as-needed`, `--maximum-zoom`, and per-layer `maxzoom` to keep the file size reasonable.

4. **Performance** – Even a combined tileset is still fetched tile-by-tile. The “single source” claim only reduces the number of HTTP requests *if* you also bundle everything into a **PMTiles** file and serve it with range requests. Otherwise you’ll still be making many tile requests, just to one domain.
## Recommended default workflow for most apps
Basemap (vector tiles)  ← hosted style URL (e.g., MapTiler, OpenFreeMap)
Delivery zones (geojson) ← your own file or API
└─ source: ""zones""     (type: ""geojson"" or a tiny vector tile source)
Style → add a fill layer for ""zones"" before the first symbol layer.
*Result:* two sources, zero extra build work, automatic basemap updates, correct OSM attribution, and instant ability to edit or replace the zones without touching the basemap.
